note: Question of the day. Added to the end of the daily queue, in this order, the first time the server sees them. Once a question's day has passed everywhere, it joins the question pool for runs.

questions.stem: Why did Apple make the buttons and bars in iOS 26 look like see-through glass?
options: Glass effects use less battery than solid colours
To match the glass backs of recent iPhones
So the controls step back and your content stays in focus
To hide design differences between older and newer apps
questions.explanationRight: Apple says Liquid Glass reflects and refracts what's behind it while bringing greater focus to content. Controls give way to what you're looking at: in iOS 26, tab bars shrink as you scroll and come back when you need them. The same material runs across iPhone, iPad, Mac, Watch and TV, so it all feels of a piece.
explanationWrong: Battery wasn't the reason, and glass effects take more work to draw, not less. Apple's aim was to let controls give way to content, so what you're reading or watching stays in focus.
The look isn't about the hardware. Apple made controls translucent and lets them shrink out of the way, so the content underneath stays the focus.
It isn't a disguise for older apps. The glass lets buttons and bars sit lightly over the content, and tab bars even shrink as you scroll, keeping the focus on what you came for.
questions.sourceName: Apple Newsroom: Apple introduces a delightful and elegant new software design (June 2025)

questions.stem: While you wait for a ride, why does Rapido tell you how many captains turned your request down?
options: Indian law makes ride apps publish every rejection
It shows the search is working, so the wait feels fair
It warns you off booking at the busiest times
Captains asked for it, to explain their choices
questions.explanationRight: Rapido has never published why, so this one is a deduction: the best explanation the evidence supports. Designers call it operational transparency: showing the work while people wait. In a Harvard study from 2011, people valued a service more when it showed the work being done, and some even preferred a longer wait with the work on show to an instant answer. A running count of captains asked tells you the app isn't stuck. Some designers point out it can also nudge riders to add a tip or accept a higher fare.
explanationWrong: No law requires it. Showing the count is Rapido's choice, and the likeliest reason is that seeing the search at work makes a wait feel fairer than staring at a spinner.
The count shows on any search, busy or not. Its job is to show the app is working for you, so the wait doesn't feel like a frozen screen.
The count is about your wait, not the captains' reasons. Seeing the search at work makes waiting feel less like being ignored.
questions.sourceName: Buell and Norton, Harvard Business School: The labor illusion (2011)

questions.stem: Why do the pages of Switzerland's 2022 passport reveal hidden contour lines and landmarks under ultraviolet light?
options: They let border staff check it in dark booths
They show which canton issued the passport
They guide blind holders to the right page
They're security marks that are very hard to forge
questions.explanationRight: Switzerland's federal police say the passport carries its most advanced security features yet, some visible to the eye and some only under UV light. The Geneva studio RETINAA made those features part of the picture: each page shows the mountains and rivers of a canton, and under UV light contour lines and landmarks appear. Ink that only shows under UV is very hard for a forger to reproduce, so the art doubles as protection.
explanationWrong: Border checks don't happen in the dark. The hidden layers are security features: they only appear under UV light, which makes the passport very hard to fake.
Each page already shows a canton's mountains and rivers in plain sight. The UV layer is a security feature, hidden so that forgers can't easily copy it.
UV images can't be felt, so they wouldn't help. They're a security feature, hidden in the design so that a fake is easy to spot and hard to make.
questions.sourceName: Le News: New Swiss passport features rivers and mountains (November 2022)

questions.stem: In 2025, why did Duolingo replace hearts, which you lost for every mistake, with energy?
options: Players outside gaming didn't understand the idea of lives
Losing hearts for mistakes punished beginners, who make the most
An energy bar takes less room on small screens
Learners asked for a way to finish lessons faster
questions.explanationRight: Duolingo said hearts weren't the best way to support learning. Every mistake cost a free learner a heart, and beginners, who are still finding their feet, were twice as likely to run out of hearts partway through a lesson. That's discouraging, since mistakes are part of learning. Energy is spent on right answers too, and a run of right answers earns some back, so the system rewards getting things right instead of only punishing slips.
explanationWrong: People understood hearts well enough. The problem Duolingo named was that hearts only ever punished mistakes, and beginners ran out twice as often, often mid-lesson.
Screen space wasn't the issue. Duolingo said losing a heart for every mistake discouraged beginners, who were twice as likely to run out partway through a lesson.
Speed wasn't the aim. Duolingo moved to energy because hearts punished mistakes, and beginners, who make the most, were running out mid-lesson.
questions.sourceName: Duolingo blog: Duolingo energy (July 2025)

questions.stem: Why did Google's 2026 icons for Docs, Drive and Meet stop using all four of its colours?
options: Four colours cost too much to print on merchandise
So each app is easier to pick out at a glance
Tiny icons blurred the four colours into a brown smudge
A court ruled the colours copied another brand's logo
questions.explanationRight: Google said the new designs give every app a more distinct identity and keep each one recognisable on your screen. Since 2020, Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs and Meet had all been drawn in the same red, yellow, green and blue, so a row of them looked alike at a glance. The 2026 icons give most apps one main colour; only Gmail keeps all four.
explanationWrong: Merchandise had nothing to do with it. Google said the change gives every app a more distinct identity, so each one is easier to recognise on a crowded screen.
The icons weren't blurring. The trouble was that they all used the same four colours, so they looked alike. Giving each app one main colour makes it easier to spot.
There was no ruling. Google changed the icons so each app has a more distinct identity and is easier to recognise at a glance.
questions.sourceName: Google Workspace Updates: A fresh visual identity for Google Workspace app icons (May 2026)

questions.stem: Why doesn't the 0 on most rulers sit right at the very end?
options: It gives your thumb a place to hold the ruler still
It leaves room for the maker to print their name
The ends get chipped, and a 0 there would chip too
Rulers need a blank end so they are safe for children
questions.hint: Think about which part of a ruler takes the most knocks.
questions.explanationRight: The ends of a ruler take the knocks: dropped on the floor, pushed against walls, rattled around in pencil cases. If the 0 sat right at the edge, every chip would move it, and every measurement after that would come out a little short. Setting the 0 a few millimetres in keeps it on the flat of the ruler, where it stays accurate long after the corners have worn round. It also means the end doesn't have to be cut perfectly when the ruler is made.
explanationWrong: You can hold a ruler anywhere, and the gap is too small to grip. The reason is wear: the ends take the knocks, so a 0 right at the edge would be chipped away and every measurement would drift. Setting it a little way in keeps it accurate.
Makers print their name along the middle, where there's plenty of room. The gap is there because the ends get chipped and worn, and a 0 at the very edge would wear away with them.
No rule asks for that, and a blank end is no blunter than a numbered one. The ends of a ruler get knocked about, so the 0 sits a little way in, where a chip can't move it.
questions.sourceName: Family Handyman: Why is there a space before the zero mark on a ruler?

image.alt: The end of a wooden ruler: the 0 mark sits a few millimetres in from the edge, with a blank strip before it.

questions.stem: Why did Heinz print a border in one exact shade of red around its ketchup labels?
options: So the bottle is easier to find on a busy table
Red makes food look tastier and makes people hungry
So diners can spot a bottle refilled with cheap ketchup
To show at a glance how full the bottle still is
questions.hint: Restaurants don't always buy a new bottle when one runs out.
questions.explanationRight: Some restaurants refill empty Heinz bottles with cheaper ketchup, so diners think they're getting Heinz and get something else. In 2023 Heinz in Turkey printed a border in the exact red of its own ketchup, Pantone 7626C, around the label. Hold the bottle up: if the sauce inside doesn't match the border, it probably isn't Heinz. The agency behind it reported far fewer refilled bottles in the street food restaurants it checked.
explanationWrong: A Heinz bottle is easy enough to spot already. The border is a colour test: it's printed in the exact red of Heinz ketchup, so if the sauce inside looks different, someone has probably refilled the bottle with a cheaper brand.

Red is common on food packaging, but this border had a sharper job. It matches the exact colour of Heinz ketchup, so if the sauce in the bottle is a different red, you know it's been refilled with something cheaper.

The border runs round the edge of the label, not up the side like a gauge. It's printed in the exact red of Heinz ketchup, so diners can check that what's inside really is Heinz and not a cheaper refill.
questions.sourceName: Contagious: Heinz cracks down on counterfeiters with ketchup colour swatch labels

questions.stem: Why do some sign-up progress bars start a little way full, before you've done anything?
options: A sliver of colour shows people where the bar is
Screens round up, so a bar never shows exactly zero
It copies video games, where you start at level 1
Starting ahead makes people more likely to finish
questions.hint: Think of a loyalty card that comes with two stamps already on it.
questions.explanationRight: People who feel they've already made progress are more likely to see a task through. In a well known study, car wash customers got loyalty cards needing 8 stamps, or cards needing 10 with 2 already stamped: the same 8 washes either way. Far more of the second group finished their cards, 34% against 19%, and they finished faster. Sign-up and set-up screens use the same trick, so a bar that starts part full keeps you going to the end.
explanationWrong: The empty track already shows where the bar is. The head start is there to motivate: people who feel they've begun are more likely to finish, the same reason loyalty cards often come with a couple of stamps already on them.
A progress bar shows whatever the designer tells it to, and zero is easy to draw. It starts part full on purpose, because feeling you've already started makes you more likely to finish.
Games aren't where it comes from. Researchers found that a head start, even a made-up one, makes people more likely to finish a task, so sign-up screens start the bar a little way along.
questions.sourceName: Nunes and Drèze: The Endowed Progress Effect, Journal of Consumer Research (2006)

image.alt: A sign-up screen with an empty form, and a progress bar that already shows step 1 of 5, 20% done.

questions.stem: Why does the Kadokeshi eraser from Japan have 28 corners?
options: Each corner is a different firmness for different pencils
It grips better, so it won't slip from your fingers
There's always a sharp corner left for tiny details
The bumps stop it rolling off a sloping desk
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the corner of an ordinary eraser after a few uses.
questions.explanationRight: A new eraser's sharp corner is perfect for rubbing out one small mark, but after a few uses it goes round and blunt, and a block only has 8 corners. The Kadokeshi, designed by Hideo Kanbara for Kokuyo in 2001, is made of little cubes joined together, which gives it 28. As one corner wears down, there's always another sharp one ready for fine details. Its name joins the Japanese words for corner and eraser, and it's in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
explanationWrong: The whole eraser is one piece of the same rubber. The shape is about corners: an ordinary eraser soon wears its 8 corners round, and the Kadokeshi's 28 mean there's always a sharp one for rubbing out small details.
It isn't a grip. The little cubes add corners, 28 of them instead of a block's 8, so as one wears blunt there's always a sharp one left for precise erasing.
An ordinary block doesn't roll either. The shape is about corners: each is a sharp point for rubbing out tiny details, and with 28 of them there's always a fresh one when the last goes round.
questions.sourceName: Kokuyo: Kadokeshi eraser

questions.stem: Why do so many lifts have mirrors?
options: Glass panels are lighter, so the lift can move faster
Waiting feels shorter when there's something to look at
Mirrors hide scratches and dents better than paint
Mirrors stay cool, so the lift needs less air conditioning
questions.hint: The complaints were about how long people waited, and the lifts never got faster.
questions.explanationRight: Waiting with nothing to do feels longer than it is. In the classic case, told about a New York office block and about a hotel group, people complained the lifts were too slow. Rather than rebuild them, the owners put up mirrors where people waited. People checked their hair and glanced at each other, the wait felt shorter, and the complaints dropped, though the lifts were no faster. Today mirrors in and around lifts are everywhere, and the same idea is behind the screens and music wherever people queue.
explanationWrong: A mirror is no lighter than the panel it replaces, and the lifts in the famous case never got faster. The mirrors worked because a wait with something to look at feels shorter, so the complaints about slow lifts stopped.

Mirrors show scratches, if anything. They went up where people waited because time with something to look at passes faster: people who had complained about slow lifts stopped, though the lifts were just as slow.
Mirrors don't cool anything. They were put where people waited, because a wait with something to look at, like your own reflection, feels shorter, and the complaints about slow lifts stopped.
questions.sourceName: David Maister: The Psychology of Waiting Lines (1985)

questions.stem: Why is there a little plastic table in the middle of a pizza?
options: It keeps the slices from sliding around
It lets steam escape from under the lid
It stops the lid sagging onto the cheese
It marks the centre for cutting even slices
questions.hint: Think about what hot steam does to a cardboard lid on the way to your door.
questions.explanationRight: A hot pizza fills its box with steam, and the steam softens the cardboard, so the middle of the lid sags down onto the cheese and toppings. The little three-legged stand holds the lid up. Carmela Vitale of Dix Hills, New York, patented it in 1985 as a "package saver", writing that box lids tend to sag at the centre and "damage or mark the pies" on the way.
explanationWrong: A stand that small can't hold the slices in place. It's there for the lid: steam from the hot pizza softens the cardboard, the lid sags onto the cheese, and the little table holds it up.
It doesn't open anything; the lid still sits on top. The steam is actually the problem: it softens the cardboard so the lid sags onto the cheese, and the little table holds it up.
Pizzas are cut before they go in the box, and the stand isn't a guide. It holds the lid up: steam softens the cardboard, and without the stand the lid sags onto the cheese.
questions.sourceName: Gizmodo: That plastic thing inside your pizza box was invented 30 years ago

image.alt: A small white three-legged plastic stand standing in the middle of a pizza.

questions.stem: Why do cash machines give your card back before the cash?
options: So the machine can check the card isn't stolen
Once people have their cash, they forget the card
Cards come out faster than counting notes
So thieves can't grab both at once
questions.hint: What were you actually there for, and what happens once you have it?
questions.explanationRight: People go to a cash machine for the cash. Early machines handed out the money first, and once people had it, the job felt finished, so many walked away and left their card behind. Psychologists call this a post-completion error, the same slip as leaving the original in a photocopier. Machines now return the card first and hold the cash until it's taken, so you can't get what you came for without taking your card. In one study, the card-first order cut lost cards to zero and made withdrawals quicker.
explanationWrong: The card is checked when you put it in, long before any cash comes out. The order is about memory: once people have their money, the job feels done, so they leave the card behind. Handing the card back first means you can't finish without it.

Speed isn't the point; the machine could count notes while you wait either way. People used to walk off with their cash and forget their card, because the job felt done. Card first, then cash, means you can't leave without it.

Returning both together wouldn't help a thief much, and that isn't the reason. People used to take their cash and walk away without their card, because getting the money felt like the end. Card first makes taking it part of getting paid.
questions.sourceName: Quality and Innovation: Practical poka-yoke

image.alt: A cash machine screen saying "Please take your card to continue with your transaction", with a drawing of a hand taking the card.

questions.stem: Why is the metal hook on a tape measure loose?
options: It wobbles so it can grip rough, uneven edges
It shifts by its own thickness, so readings are exact
The rivets work loose over time as the tape wears
So it can fold flat against the case
questions.hint: Measure a box by hooking the end over its edge. Now measure inside a drawer by pushing the end against the wall.
questions.explanationRight: The hook has a thickness of its own, about 1/16 of an inch, and that would throw off every measurement one way or the other. Hook it over an edge and it slides out by exactly its thickness; push it against a wall and it slides in, so the thickness counts. Either way the reading starts from a true zero. The wobble people try to fix is the feature.
explanationWrong: The hook moves along the tape, not side to side, and only by a tiny, set amount. That amount is the hook's own thickness: it slides out when you hook an edge and in when you push against a wall, so the reading is exact both ways.

It's loose from the day it's made, on purpose. The hook slides by exactly its own thickness, out when hooked over an edge and in when pushed against a surface, so every reading starts from a true zero.
The hook doesn't fold; it moves a tiny set distance along the tape. That distance is the hook's own thickness, so the reading is right whether you hook an edge or push against a wall.
questions.sourceName: Family Handyman: Why the end of your tape measure is loose

image.alt: The end of a yellow tape measure, close up: the metal hook held by two rivets in slots, loose enough to slide.

questions.stem: Why do crackers have rows of small holes?
options: They make the cracker lighter to pack
Steam escapes, so they bake flat, not puffy
They help butter and toppings soak in
They're just a decorative pattern
questions.hint: What happens to a thin sheet of wet dough when it heats up fast in an oven?
questions.explanationRight: Cracker dough holds water, and in a hot oven that water turns to steam. Trapped steam puffs the dough into bubbles and pillows, like a pitta. So before baking, the dough passes under a roller of pins, called a docker, that punches the holes. The steam escapes through them and the cracker bakes flat and crisp. The spacing is tuned: too close and the cracker dries out hard, too far apart and bubbles rise between the holes.
explanationWrong: The holes weigh almost nothing either way. They're there for the steam: water in the dough turns to steam in the oven, and without a way out it puffs the cracker into bubbles.
Toppings sit on top; the holes are far too small to soak anything up. They let steam out while the cracker bakes, so it stays flat and crisp instead of puffing up.
The pattern looks deliberate because it is, but for baking, not looks. Each hole lets steam escape in the oven, and the spacing is tuned so no bubbles rise between them.
questions.sourceName: Today I Found Out: Why crackers have holes

image.alt: A square golden cracker with neat rows of small holes across it.

questions.stem: Why does a car's rear-view mirror have a little tab underneath?
options: It locks the mirror so it can't be knocked
It turns on a light for reading maps
Flicked at night, it dims dazzling headlights behind
It releases the mirror for cleaning
questions.hint: Driving at night, what behind you could shine straight into your eyes?
questions.explanationRight: At night, the headlights of the car behind shine into the rear-view mirror and straight into your eyes. The mirror's glass is a wedge, thicker at one edge, with the silvered surface at the back. Normally you see that bright back surface. Flick the tab and the mirror tilts, so the bright reflection goes up to the roof and you see a much dimmer one from the plain glass at the front: enough to see the cars behind, without the glare.
explanationWrong: It doesn't lock anything; the mirror stays as easy to move. The tab tilts a wedge of glass, so at night you see a dim reflection from its front surface instead of the bright mirror behind it, and headlights stop dazzling you.
Map lights have their own switches. The tab tilts the mirror's wedge-shaped glass, so at night the bright reflection goes up to the roof and you see a dimmer one that doesn't dazzle.
The mirror doesn't come off there. The tab is for night driving: it tilts the wedge-shaped glass so the dazzling headlights behind you reflect away, leaving a dim image you can still use.
questions.sourceName: Science World: How does the rearview mirror antiglare work?

image.alt: A hand reaching for the small tab on the underside of a car's rear-view mirror, circled in red.

questions.stem: Why do sachets have a tiny V-shaped cut at one edge?
options: It lets air out when the sachet is sealed
It starts the tear, so you don't need scissors
It marks the batch number for the factory
It shows which end holds the most product
questions.hint: Try tearing a sachet anywhere else along its edge.
questions.explanationRight: Sachet film is made to be tough: it has to survive filling machines, shipping and pockets. That same toughness makes smooth plastic hard to rip open by hand, because a tear needs somewhere to start. The little V-cut is that start, made at the factory. Pull at the notch and the tear runs across in a clean line, no scissors or teeth needed.
explanationWrong: Sachets are sealed with heat, not by pushing air out through a cut. The V is a head start for your fingers: tough film is hard to rip open, and the notch gives the tear somewhere to begin.
Batch numbers are printed, not cut. The notch is where you open it: tough plastic film is hard to tear by hand until a tear has somewhere to start.
The contents settle anywhere. The notch is a starting point for the tear, so you can open the sachet without scissors.
questions.sourceName: Packerio: What is a tear notch and why does it matter for your packaging?
questions.pictureBrief: A shampoo or ketchup sachet close up, the small V-shaped notch at its edge in view.

questions.stem: Why do hotel room lights only work with your key card in a slot?
options: It proves to reception that you've checked in
So nothing's left running when you go out
It charges the key card so it keeps working
It unlocks the minibar and the safe
questions.hint: What happens to the lights and air conditioning when you walk out with the card?
questions.explanationRight: Guests pay for the room, not the electricity, so plenty of them leave the lights, fan and air conditioning running all day while they're out. Hotels fixed it with the one thing every guest has to take with them: the key card. It sits in a slot by the door that switches the room's power on, and when you take it out to leave, the power goes off a few seconds later. Makers of these switches say they can cut a room's energy costs by up to 30 percent.
explanationWrong: Check-in is recorded when the card is made at the desk. The slot is a power switch: take the card out to leave, and the lights and air conditioning switch off behind you.
Hotel key cards don't need charging. The slot switches the room's power on, so the moment you take your card and go, nothing is left running in an empty room.
The minibar and safe have their own locks. The slot is the room's power switch: the card you must take with you is what turns everything off when you leave.
questions.sourceName: Ecolabel Toolbox: Key card systems that switch off electricity in rooms
questions.pictureBrief: The key card slot on the wall by a hotel room door, with a card in it.

questions.stem: Why do fizzy drink bottles have bumpy feet, but water bottles flat bottoms?
options: The feet help the bottle grip wet surfaces
Gas pressure would bulge a flat bottom so it rocks
The bumps tell sugary drinks apart from water
The feet let cold air around it to chill it
questions.hint: Squeeze a sealed bottle of fizzy drink. Which way is the gas pushing?
questions.explanationRight: The gas in a fizzy drink presses outward on every part of the bottle, at two or three times the pressure in a car tyre. A flat plastic bottom would be pushed out into a dome, and the bottle would rock or tip over. The petal-shaped feet take that force into the valleys between them, while their tips give the bottle something steady to stand on. Still water has no gas pushing out, so its bottle can keep a simple flat bottom.
explanationWrong: The feet only touch the table at their tips, so they grip no better. They're there because gas presses outward inside a fizzy drink, and a flat plastic base would bulge until the bottle rocked.
Labels already tell drinks apart. The shape is about pressure: the gas in a fizzy drink pushes the base outward, and the petal feet stop it bulging into a rocker.
Chilling has nothing to do with it. Gas pressure inside a fizzy drink would push a flat base out into a dome; the petal shape takes that force and keeps the bottle standing.
questions.sourceName: iBottler: Why do soda bottles have that 5-point base?
questions.pictureBrief: The bottom of a plastic fizzy drink bottle, its five petal-shaped feet in view, beside a flat-bottomed water bottle.

questions.stem: Why can Gmail undo an email a few seconds after you hit Send?
options: It deletes the email from the other person's inbox
It hasn't sent it yet: it waits a few seconds
Emails take a few minutes to travel between servers
It only undoes emails nobody has opened yet
questions.hint: Could Gmail reach into someone else's inbox, or does the trick happen before that?
questions.explanationRight: Once an email lands in someone else's inbox, Gmail can't take it back. So Undo works by not sending it straight away. When you hit Send, Gmail holds the message for a few seconds (you choose 5, 10, 20 or 30 in settings) and only then delivers it. Press Undo during that wait and the delivery is simply cancelled, and the message goes back to your drafts. The Send button is, quietly, a countdown.
explanationWrong: Gmail can't reach into another inbox once the email arrives. The trick is waiting: it holds your message for a few seconds after you hit Send, so Undo cancels a delivery that hasn't happened.
Emails usually arrive in seconds. Undo works because Gmail deliberately waits a few seconds before sending, and cancels the delivery if you change your mind.
Whether anyone has read it makes no difference. The message was never sent yet: Gmail holds it for a few seconds after you press Send, and Undo cancels that.
questions.sourceName: Gmail Help: Undo sending mail
questions.pictureBrief: Gmail's 'Message sent' notice at the bottom of the screen, with its Undo button.

questions.stem: Why do many hospital and office doors have a narrow window at eye level?
options: It stops the door warping in damp weather
So you see someone coming before you swing it open
It makes the heavy door lighter to push
Glass lets the air conditioning reach both sides
questions.hint: Think about two people reaching the same door from opposite sides.
questions.explanationRight: A door that swings into a busy corridor can hit whoever is on the other side: a nurse with a tray, a child, someone in a wheelchair. A small window lets both people see each other before anyone pushes. Building rules in many countries ask for one on doors that swing both ways or cut across corridors, set low enough for children and wheelchair users to see through too. In a fire, it also lets you check what's behind a door before you open it.
explanationWrong: Doors are built to cope with damp either way. The narrow window is there so you can see a person coming on the other side before you push the door into them.
A small pane saves very little weight. The window is there so people on both sides can see each other before one of them swings the door into the other.
Air doesn't pass through glass. The window lets you see someone on the other side, so nobody gets hit when a door swings open into a busy corridor.
questions.sourceName: Wikipedia: Vision panel
questions.pictureBrief: A door in a corridor with a narrow vertical window at eye level, ideally with someone visible on the other side.
